description:
MISHEK is a Guatemalan team built around computational civil engineering: the idea that infrastructure problems — on Earth or on Mars — are solved faster when engineering judgment meets data and code.

Christell García (project lead) is a third-year Civil Engineering student at Universidad del Valle de Guatemala.

The team is completed by  Ian Castellanos a final-year Applied Mathematics student.

"In a new place: where can a human safely walk on Mars? "
summary: AREO EVA is a hyperlocal mission-planning map system for the first Marswalks. We designed a complete, safety-driven EVA route on whe western rim of Jezero Crater using only real NASA data: the USGS Mars Sample Return Terrain Relative Navigation HiRISE mosaics (1-m DTM, 25-cm orthoimage), Mars Odyssey THEMIS day/night therman mosaics, CRISM mineralogy, and the USGS DTM-confidence product. In QGIS we fused slope (Horn, 3-m baseline), surface roughness, thermal soil firmness, and data confidence into a walking-time cost surface, solved the optimal astronaut route by Least Cost Path, and derived 15-120 minute isochones plus a verified 3-km walk-back envelope. The 3476-m route reaches the ejecta of a fresh 2-km crater (a natural drill hole into Jezero´s ancient crust) never exceeding 14.9% slope. Derivables are an interactive web map, a helmet HUD concept, and a fully reproducible QGIS project.
details:
What it does: AREO EVA turns raw NASA orbital data into an operational answer to the life or death question: where exactly can a human walk on Mars? For a 6.0 x 6.5 km area on the western rim of Jezero Crater we built a layered, pedestrian-scale map and computed a safe EVA route from a base A to a science target B. The ejecta blanket of a fresh 2-km crater, which exposes deep subsurface rock like a natural drill hole.

How it works: From the 1-m HiRISE STM we derived slope (Horn operator at a 3-m stride baseline) and RMS roughness (5-, windos, a proxy for subpixel boulder fields, verified against the 25-cm orthoimage). THEMIS nighttime infrared provides relative soil firmness (thermal inertia), and the USGS Figure of Merit confidence raster flags unreliable DTM pixels as risk. These are fused into a cost surface measured in walking time per meter, using a Tobler-type speed function adapted to a suited astronaut (2.5 km/h flat, 150-kg suit). Slopes of and above 15% are absolute no go cells and the ones in between 12-15% are a penalized caution zone. The route is solved by Least Cost Path (equivalent to GRASS r.cost/r.drain), and the accumulated-cost ifeld yield 15-120 min isochones and a verified 3-km walk-back envelope. Result: 3476 m, 123 min one way, +137 m of climb, max slope 14.9%, EVA budget of aproximately 5h 10 min including 60 min of science.

Creativity & Rigor: Our core innovation is a feature-fusion framework because instead of a single slope filter, four independent terrain descriptors (topographic slope, sub-pixel roughness, thermal soil firmness from THEMIS night IR, and the USGS data-confidence raster) are normalized and fused into one cost surface whose unit is walking time adapted to the biomechanics of a suited astronaut. This makes every trade-off physical interpretable since the optimizer literally minimizes minutes of EVA life support. Two further choices set the project apart: data quality is treated as terrain hazard (low-confidence DTM pixels are penalized like rough ground), and we documented a negative result honestly — no targeted CRISM hyperspectral observation covers the AOI (the nearest, FRT00005850, begins ~700 m east), so it is integrated as regional mineralogical context rather than forced onto the map. As future work, the framework extends naturally to object-based terrain units (watershed-delimited slope units) for route segmentation.

Tools: QGIS 3.44 LTR, GDAL, GRASS-equivalent least-cost analysis, Python (NumPy/SciPy/scikit-image, matplotlib), Leaflet for the interactive web map, LaTeX for the technical report, Canva for the presentation. AI assistance (Claude by Anthropic) was used for code generation and the HUD mockup, clearly disclosed and watermarked; data acquisition, QGIS methodology, verification and all mission decisions were made by the team.

Impact: The workflow is transferable to any site on Mars with HiRISE stereo coverage. This is a template for planning real Marswalks where safety dictates the path and science drives the destination.
